newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court says Tapie must quit Euro parliament.
newsitem.headline: French court says Tapie must quit Euro parliament.

text.p: France's top administrative court rejected on Wednesday a bid by bankrupt businessman Bernard Tapie to retain his seat in the European Parliament, his last political job.

The Council of State turned down Tapie's request to suspend a French government decree removing him from the Strasbourg parliament after a court declared him ineligible for public office on bankruptcy charges.
The Council of State ruled that a conviction for bankruptcy carried ineligibility, and national authorities were entitled to end the European mandate of ineligible representatives.

The ruling, released to the press, appeared to spell the end of the political road for Tapie, a flamboyant ex-cabinet minister who has already been stripped of his seat in the French National Assembly.
The European Parliament is expected to rule on Tapie's fate next month.

It had deferred a decision to strip him of his seat after his lawyers argued that Prime Minister Alain Juppe's decree, issued last November, was unprecedented in the history of the assembly and created a situation not provided for in its rules.

Tapie, the target of a blizzard of legal actions over his now destroyed business empire and the Marseille soccer team he once ran, has been sentenced to jail terms of eight and six months for tax fraud and rigging a soccer match.

He is appealing in both cases to the French supreme court and has promised to resign from the European Parliament if the court confirms his sentence for match-rigging at the Olympique Marseille. The ruling is expected on February 4.

His political and business career in tatters, Tapie bounced back last year by starring as a morally dubious lawyer in "Men and Women: Instructions for Use", a film by prize-winning director Claude Lelouch.
But in a further humiliation, court-appointed liquidators seeking to track down his assets to cover his debts said they would try to seize his three million francs ($585,000) earnings.
